svg.title: A 91-year-old man is in the last days of life. At 0200 the nurse turned him onto his side, gave mouth care, stopped the maintenance intravenous fluid as ordered, and taught his daughter about the gurgling sound. At 0400 the gurgling is quieter, his face is relaxed, and his daughter is sitting with him holding his hand.
svg.desc: National Cancer Institute guidance says repositioning often helps noisy terminal secretions and that limiting intravenous hydration in the final days reduces them. A quieter sound with a relaxed face and a settled family are the outcomes that matter in comfort care; an oxygen saturation is not a goal here and is the tempting wrong choice for a student used to numbers. Deep suctioning can trigger the gag reflex and be counterproductive, so it stays off the plan. Families are taught that the sound is not known to distress the dying person.
